ety.text: Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́)bor. Latin māchinabor. Middle French machinebor. English machine Borrowed from Middle French machine, from Latin māchina (“a machine, engine, contrivance, device, stratagem, trick”), from Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́), cognate with Attic Greek μηχᾰνή (mēkhănḗ, “a machine, engine, contrivance, device”), from which comes mechanical. Displaced native Old English searu.

senses.d: A device that directs and controls energy, often in the form of movement or electricity, to produce a certain effect.
A vehicle operated mechanically, such as an automobile or an airplane.
An answering machine or, by extension, voice mail.
ex: I called you earlier, but all I got was the machine.

senses.d: A computer.
ex: Game developers assume they're pushing the limits of the machine.
He refuses to turn off his Linux machine.

senses.d: A person or organisation that seemingly acts like a machine, being particularly efficient, single-minded, or unemotional.
ex: Bruce Campbell was a "demon-killing machine" because he made quick work of killing demons.
The government has become a money-making machine.

senses.d: Especially, the group that controls a political or similar organization; a combination of persons acting together for a common purpose, with the agencies which they use.
ex: The whole machine of government, civil and religious, ought never to bear upon the people with a weight so oppressive

senses.d: Supernatural agency in a poem, or a superhuman being introduced to perform some exploit.
ex: I am apt to think, that the changing of the Trojan fleet into water-nymphs, which is the most violent machine in the whole Æneid[…]

senses.d: The system of special interest groups that supports a political party, especially in urban areas.
Penis.
A contrivance in the Ancient Greek theatre for indicating a change of scene, by means of which a god might cross the stage or deliver a divine message; the deus ex machina.
To make by machinery.
To shape or finish by machinery; (usually, more specifically) to shape subtractively by metal-cutting with machine-controlled toolpaths.

grp.label: a person who is very proficient

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French machine, borrowed from Latin machina (“a machine, engine, contrivance, device, stratagem, trick”), itself a borrowing from Doric Ancient Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́). Not to be confused with machin, which means "thing".
Borrowed from Latin machina (“engine, device, mill”), from Ancient Greek μαχανά (makhaná). Compare the inherited doublet macina (“grindstone”).

senses.d: Very large in scale or scope.
In the context of macrophilia, one who is abnormally very large.
A comparatively human-friendly abbreviation of complex input to a computer program.
ex: The preprocessor expands any embedded macros into source code before it is compiled.
A recurring theme in this book is to record an Excel macro and then show how to adapt the recorded code.

senses.d: To use a macro.
ex: Do this poison thing gradually increasing potency until you hit about 78 then macro on a ghost to GM
Ok, i have to admit i macroed for 3 lvls to get my magic defence sorted :(

senses.d: To use a macro on (something).
ex: He said he macroed anatomy from 0 to about 80 and his healing went from the 52 he started with to 58.2.
For that matter, you can do something by killing the character being macroed. :) It IS Darktide after all.

senses.d: The machines constituting a production apparatus, in a plant etc., collectively.
The working parts of a machine as a group.
The collective parts of something which allow it to function.
ex: All of the machinery of the law was brought to bear on the investigation.

senses.d: The literary devices used in a work, notably for dramatic effect.

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”) (whence machine).
